source_user: Define decode and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer: Decode is the autoregressive serving phase in which the model generates the next token from the prompt and previously generated tokens, usually one token per iteration. Mechanism: each iteration reads the model weights and the per-layer KV cache, computes attention for the new position, and appends that position's K/V vectors to the cache. It matters because repeated weight/cache traffic and scheduler batching can dominate inter-token latency and limit concurrent requests. Boundary condition: decode is not always memory-bound; batch size, kernels, quantization, context length, hardware, and cache residency can shift the bottleneck. Measure prefill separately and report decode tokens/s, median and p95 inter-token latency, peak memory, cache occupancy, batch/concurrency, and utilization under fixed model, precision, tokenizer, and sampling settings.
risks: Decode bottlenecks vary with context length, batching, kernels, precision, and hardware.
Conflating prefill with decode or comparing different cache states can misattribute latency.
evidence_required: Separate profiler traces and repeated measurements for prefill and decode, including cache bytes, memory traffic, utilization, and tail latency.

source_user: Define decode and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer: In LLM serving, decode is the repeated autoregressive phase after prefill: the model selects a next token, then uses it as context for the next step. The concrete mechanism is incremental attention: the new token's queries attend to previously stored per-layer keys and values, while its own keys and values are appended to the KV cache, avoiding recomputation of earlier positions. This phase matters for user-visible inter-token latency and throughput because weight reads, KV-cache reads, and scheduling occur at every step. Boundary condition: KV-cache growth can become a capacity or bandwidth problem, but the dominant resource depends on model, context, batch, precision, kernels, and hardware. Benchmark fixed prompt/output lengths with warm-up, report median/p95 inter-token latency, tokens/s, memory, and concurrency, and keep prefill latency separate.
risks: A long context or many concurrent sequences may cause cache eviction, paging, or OOM.
Different sampling, batching, or cache policies make decode comparisons non-equivalent.
evidence_required: Matched sweeps over context length, output length, batch/concurrency, precision, and cache policy with profiler and p95 latency.

source_user: Contrast decode with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer: Decode is an incremental autoregressive implementation: after prefill, each step processes only the newly generated position, attends to the stored prior K/V entries, and appends one new K/V entry per layer. A naive implementation that does not use incremental decode may rerun the full prefix through the transformer for every new token, rebuilding prior activations/K/V; its work and memory traffic grow unnecessarily with sequence length. Boundary condition: this contrast assumes an exactly compatible reusable prefix and a runtime that supports KV caching; cache capacity, unsupported positional settings, or changed tokens can force recomputation or reduce the benefit. Compare matched model, tokenizer, precision, prompt/output lengths, batch, and hardware, measuring prefill, decode latency, tokens/s, peak memory, and cache traffic separately.
risks: A naive baseline may differ in kernels or batching, so speedup cannot be attributed solely to caching.
Cache storage can trade lower compute for higher memory use and capacity pressure.
evidence_required: Profiler-backed matched comparison across context lengths and concurrency, with K/V allocation, recomputation, latency, and memory recorded.

source_user: Contrast decode with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer: With incremental decode, prefill computes the prompt once; each later step computes the new position, reads prior keys/values from the KV cache through attention, and appends the new position's keys/values. Without that mechanism, a naive full-sequence implementation reprocesses all prior tokens for every generated token, increasing redundant attention and projection work as the context grows. Boundary condition: caching helps only when the prefix and model/position configuration are compatible and the cache remains resident; a changed prefix, eviction, or unsupported runtime may require recomputation. Use identical tokenization, weights, precision, prompt/output lengths, batch, and sampling, then measure separate prefill/decode latency, p95 inter-token latency, peak memory, and cache hits.
risks: The no-cache implementation may have different kernels or memory behavior, invalidating a simple speedup claim.
Large caches can reduce concurrency through memory pressure.
evidence_required: Repeated matched context-length and concurrency sweeps with profiler traces, cache-hit status, memory, and tail latency.

source_user: Contrast decode with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer: Incremental decode generates tokens step by step while reusing the prompt and earlier generated tokens' K/V state. Concretely, the new query attends to cached keys and values, and only the new token's per-layer keys and values are computed and appended. A naive full-prefix pass recomputes projections and attention state for all prior positions on every step, so redundant work rises with context length. Boundary condition: the cache is reusable only for a compatible exact prefix, model, positional setup, and resident capacity; otherwise recomputation or partial reuse may occur. Validate the contrast with fixed weights, tokenizer, precision, hardware, prompt/output lengths, and concurrency; record cache hits, prefill/decode times, p50/p95 inter-token latency, tokens/s, and peak memory.
risks: Cache hits and prefix compatibility must be verified rather than assumed.
Memory pressure and different execution kernels can obscure the compute-saving effect.
evidence_required: A matched profiler comparison showing K/V recomputation versus reuse across context lengths and cache capacities.

source_user: Contrast decode with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer: Decode is the cache-aware incremental path: after prompt prefill, each iteration evaluates the new position, reads earlier K/V entries for attention, and appends the new K/V entries. A naive path that reruns the complete prompt-plus-output prefix for each token does not reuse that state, causing repeated computation and usually increasing latency as the prefix grows. Boundary condition: this is not a guaranteed win if the cache is evicted, the prefix is not exactly compatible, the runtime cannot reuse it, or cache memory reduces batching enough to offset compute savings. Hold model revision, tokenizer, precision, hardware, lengths, and scheduler policy constant; measure prefill separately and compare decode latency distributions, tokens/s, peak/cache memory, and cache-hit rate.
risks: Cache memory can lower feasible concurrency and alter scheduler behavior.
End-to-end latency includes prefill, queueing, and sampling, not just decode compute.
evidence_required: Controlled cache-on/cache-off or equivalent matched runs with queueing, cache status, profiler data, and p95/p99 latency.

source_user: Contrast decode with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer: In incremental decode, the prompt is processed once and each new token uses attention over stored prior keys/values, appending only its own per-layer K/V vectors. A naive implementation without this reuse feeds the entire growing sequence through the model for each token, recomputing prior projections and attention state. Thus the mechanisms differ in redundant work, memory traffic, and latency scaling with context length. Boundary condition: reuse requires an exact compatible prefix and sufficient cache capacity; changed tokens, different positional/model settings, eviction, or unsupported kernels can invalidate the comparison. Benchmark both paths with identical model, tokenizer, precision, hardware, prompt/output lengths, and batch; report prefill and decode separately, plus cache bytes, peak memory, throughput, median/p95 latency, and utilization.
risks: Different implementations may use unequal optimizations or kernels.
Cache allocation and long contexts may cause OOM or lower concurrency.
evidence_required: Profiler traces and repeated matched sweeps demonstrating recomputation, cache reuse, memory, and latency scaling.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with decode. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer: Two failure modes/trade-offs are: (1) KV-cache growth can exhaust device memory or trigger paging/eviction, reducing concurrency or forcing recomputation; and (2) decode can become memory-bandwidth- or scheduler-bound, so adding batch size may improve utilization but worsen per-request tail inter-token latency. Mechanism: each step reads prior K/V entries for attention and appends the new position's K/V, while repeatedly accessing weights. Boundary condition: neither failure is universal—short contexts, small batches, quantization, kernels, and hardware can shift the bottleneck. Diagnose with fixed model and workload while recording cache occupancy/evictions, peak memory, memory traffic, utilization, queueing, tokens/s, and p50/p95/p99 inter-token latency; separate prefill from decode.
risks: Tail latency can be dominated by queueing rather than token computation.
OOM, eviction, or paging behavior may change the workload during measurement.
evidence_required: Profiler and serving telemetry for cache bytes/evictions, memory bandwidth, queueing, utilization, and latency distributions across concurrency.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with decode. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer: Two important trade-offs are: (1) caching prior K/V state avoids recomputing the prefix but consumes memory proportional to layers, heads, sequence length, batch, and precision, potentially reducing concurrency or causing eviction/OOM; and (2) continuous batching can raise aggregate tokens/s by sharing work, but queueing and interference can increase an individual request's p95/p99 inter-token latency. Mechanism: each decode step reads the accumulated K/V cache and appends the new token's entries. Boundary condition: the severity depends on context length, batch/concurrency, cache policy, kernels, and hardware, so it cannot be inferred from model size alone. Measure cache occupancy, evictions, peak memory, queueing, tokens/s, and latency quantiles under matched load, with prefill and decode timed separately.
risks: Throughput improvements can hide unacceptable tail latency.
Cache precision and allocator fragmentation can alter capacity and failure thresholds.
evidence_required: Load sweeps with cache telemetry, allocator/memory data, queueing delay, utilization, and p50/p95/p99 decode latency.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with decode. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Decode generates one or a few tokens per step and repeatedly reads model weights and KV state; it is often sensitive to memory bandwidth and scheduling.
corrected_answer: Two failure modes/trade-offs are: (1) as sequences grow, the KV cache consumes more device memory; eviction, paging, or allocation failure can force recomputation, reduce concurrency, or cause OOM; and (2) batching improves hardware utilization and aggregate throughput but can increase queueing and inter-token tail latency, especially for heterogeneous sequence lengths. Mechanism: attention reads cached keys/values for every new token and appends new entries, so traffic and cache footprint grow with context. Boundary condition: these effects depend on runtime kernels, precision, hardware, cache policy, and workload; short contexts may be compute-bound instead. Use warm-up and repeated matched load tests, separating prefill/decode and recording cache hits/evictions, memory, utilization, queueing, tokens/s, and latency quantiles.
risks: Mixed prompt/output lengths confound batching and cache-growth effects.
A cache failure can change execution mode, so post-failure measurements are not comparable to normal decode.
evidence_required: Controlled concurrency and length sweeps with profiler traces plus cache, allocator, queueing, throughput, and p95/p99 latency telemetry.
